code.title: Promise runs eagerly; Observable is lazy and cancellable

followUps:
A cold Observable creates a fresh producer for every subscriber; a hot one shares a producer that is already running.

Cold: http.get(url) fires a new request per subscribe, like pressing play on your own copy of a video. Hot: a click stream or WebSocket keeps going whether or not anyone listens, like live TV; late subscribers miss earlier values. Turn cold into hot with share() or shareReplay(). Two subscribers to a cold request mean two HTTP calls.

It returned a Promise of the last value but silently hid what happens when the stream is empty or never completes, so it was deprecated in RxJS 7 and is slated for removal in 8.

Use firstValueFrom(obs$) when you want the first value (it unsubscribes right away) or lastValueFrom(obs$) for the last one on completion. Both make the choice explicit, and both reject with EmptyError on an empty stream unless you pass { defaultValue }.

Because switchMap cancels the previous inner request when a new value arrives, so an earlier write can be dropped from the view of your app even though the server may already have processed it.

A POST that already reached the server may still be saved, yet your app never sees its response. Click Save twice quickly: the first save may succeed unnoticed and the UI shows only the second. For writes use concatMap (ordered) or exhaustMap (ignore repeats).

concatMap(fn) is the same as mergeMap(fn, 1): a concurrency limit of one means each inner Observable must finish before the next starts, so values queue in order.

Example: source emits A, B, C quickly and each inner takes 100 ms. With mergeMap(fn, 1) the results arrive at 100, 200, 300 ms, in order A, B, C. With mergeMap(fn, 2) A and B run together and C waits for a free slot.

Because operators after it would not be cleaned up: takeUntilDestroyed completes the stream at the point where it sits, and an operator placed after it can still hold a subscription to another stream.

For example takeUntilDestroyed() before switchMap(...) stops the outer source, but the inner request created by switchMap keeps running. Put it last and the complete signal reaches every inner stream. Linting rules (e.g. rxjs-no-unsafe-takeuntil) enforce this.

Usually no: HttpClient Observables emit once and then complete, and completion releases the subscription, so nothing leaks.

You still unsubscribe (or use takeUntilDestroyed) when you want to cancel a slow request that is no longer needed, for instance when the user leaves the page, which aborts the XHR or fetch. Note that a response arriving after the component is destroyed can still run your callback and touch dead state, so cancelling is a good habit.

code.title: Subject, BehaviorSubject and ReplaySubject for late subscribers

followUps:
After complete() a plain Subject gives a late subscriber only the complete notification; a BehaviorSubject does the same (it does not replay its value once completed); a ReplaySubject replays its buffered values and then completes.

Example: values 1,2,3 then complete, new subscriber: Subject gets just complete, BehaviorSubject gets just complete, ReplaySubject(2) gets 2, 3, complete. That is why ReplaySubject suits caches and BehaviorSubject does not survive completion.

So outsiders can only read, not push values; the service stays the single owner of state changes.

If a component receives the Subject itself it can call next() with anything and break invariants, which makes bugs hard to trace. Keep private _user$ = new BehaviorSubject(null) and expose user$ = this._user$.asObservable(). The type has no next, and with signals the same idea is asReadonly().

code.title: A tiny signal, computed and effect with tracking

followUps:
Because an effect that writes a signal creates a second, hidden update step, which risks loops and extra change detection; derived state is what computed is for.

With effect(() => this.full.set(first() + last())) the value is stale until the effect flushes, and it can run extra times. Writing full = computed(() => first() + last()) is synchronous, memoized and never needs a write. Since Angular 19 writes inside effects are allowed by default, but they are still discouraged for this reason.

untracked(() => ...) reads signals without registering them as dependencies, so a change in them does not re-run the effect or computed.

Example: effect(() => { log(user().id, untracked(() => theme())); }) re-runs when the user changes but not when the theme changes. Use it for context values you need to read but not react to.

Because toObservable uses an effect, so it only emits the latest value when the effect flushes, not every intermediate write.

If you do s.set(1); s.set(2); s.set(3) in one tick, the Observable emits only 3. This is right for state but wrong for events, where every occurrence matters. For event streams keep a Subject. Also, emission is asynchronous, so a synchronous read right after set sees nothing yet.

Choose a Subject when each occurrence matters, not just the current state: clicks, "save requested", WebSocket messages, or a destroy notifier.

Signals coalesce writes and skip equal values, so three identical "refresh" commands become one. A Subject delivers all three, supports operators like debounce and switchMap, and has no required current value. Rule of thumb: state is a signal, events are Subjects.

Because debouncing the input stops the keystrokes from becoming requests at all, while debouncing the HTTP call would still send each request first.

Typing "angular" fast produces 7 values. Debounce on the input with 300 ms waits for a pause and sends 1 request. Without it, 7 requests start and switchMap cancels 6, still wasting work and sometimes server load. Apply debounceTime before switchMap.

Use a fake clock so no real time passes, and assert what was emitted at each virtual moment.

With Jasmine fakeAsync call tick(299) and expect no request, then tick(1) and expect exactly one request with the latest text. RxJS also offers TestScheduler with marble diagrams. Also test that quick typing sends one call and that a new term cancels the old one.

The async pipe calls markForCheck() on every emission, which tells Angular this OnPush view needs checking; a plain field assignment inside subscribe does not.

An OnPush component re-renders only on input change, DOM events from its template, or when marked dirty. A subscribe callback that does this.items = x changes data but marks nothing, so the screen stays stale (under zone.js it may still look fine when another event triggers a check). Fix by using async pipe, signals, or calling cdr.markForCheck().

It still works, because it calls markForCheck on each emission and Angular schedules a check from that notification, with no zone.js needed.

That is why async pipe and signals are the safe choices for zoneless apps. A manual subscribe that sets a plain field fails there: nothing schedules change detection. Setting a signal inside the callback does work.

code.title: retry with backoff, only for transient errors

followUps:
The second argument is caught, the source Observable itself, so returning it re-subscribes and effectively retries.

Example: catchError((err, caught) => attempts++ < 3 ? caught : throwError(() => err)) retries up to three times. It is handy but easy to loop forever without a counter, so retry({ count, delay }) is usually clearer.

Jitter adds a small random amount to each wait so that many clients do not all retry at the same instant after an outage.

Without it, 1000 clients that failed together all retry at 1 s, then all at 2 s, creating repeated load spikes on a recovering server. With delay = base * 2^n * random(0.5..1) the retries spread out. Cap the maximum delay and the attempt count.

code.title: Version-based push-pull: no glitch, equality cutoff

followUps:
Because most derived values are never read, and laziness means you pay only for what is actually used and only at the moment it is needed.

If a computed does a costly filter of 10,000 items and the template hides it, a lazy computed never runs. It also lets the framework read dependencies in order and avoid computing from half-updated inputs. An eager design would recompute on every write.

The error is cached and rethrown on every read until a dependency changes, then it tries again.

For example computed(() => JSON.parse(text())) throws on bad text; reading it again does not re-run the parse, it rethrows the same error. When text becomes valid, the next read recomputes. An effect reading it will throw too, so guard or catch inside the computed.

With refCount: true the source is unsubscribed when the last subscriber leaves; with false it stays subscribed forever and keeps the cached value.

Use true for streams that should stop when unused (polling, sockets). Use false for one-shot HTTP caches you want to keep. With true, a new subscriber after everyone left starts the source again, causing a fresh request.

Yes: httpResource or resource is created once as a field, and the template reads its signals, so reading them many times never restarts the request.

The request reruns only when the signals it depends on change, and it tracks value(), isLoading() and error() for you. That removes the multiple-subscribe class of bug, since there is no cold Observable to subscribe to repeatedly.

onCleanup registers a function that runs before the effect re-runs and when it is destroyed, so you can undo what the last run started.

Example: effect((onCleanup) => { const id = setInterval(tick, query()); onCleanup(() => clearInterval(id)); }). When query changes, the old interval is cleared first, then a new one starts; without it you would stack timers.

Create the component or service in the TestBed, change signals, and then call TestBed.tick() (or fixture.detectChanges()) to flush effects, then assert.

Effects are asynchronous, so asserting straight after set sees the old result. In older versions use TestBed.flushEffects(). Prefer testing the observable outcome (what was written to storage) rather than the effect function itself.

When you need strict, auditable event flow: every change is a named action, reducers are pure, and tools can replay or time-travel through history.

That pays off for large teams, complex cross-feature workflows, and apps needing devtools or action logging. For a medium app it adds boilerplate (actions, reducers, effects, selectors) that a signal store avoids. NgRx SignalStore gives a lighter middle ground.

Keep the same public API while swapping the internals, and move consumers over one at a time.

Step 1: hold the state in a private signal and keep user$ = toObservable(this.user) so old callers still work. Step 2: add a readonly user signal for new code. Step 3: convert components, then drop the Observable. Watch that toObservable emits asynchronously and only the latest value, which can differ from BehaviorSubject.
